newsitem.title: GERMANY: Curious 10,000 get peek at new Mercedes A-class.
newsitem.headline: Curious 10,000 get peek at new Mercedes A-class.

text.p: Curiosity got the better of about 10,000 people in Frankfurt on Wednesday as carmaker Mercedes-Benz AG opened up an unusual six-storey cube in the city centre to show off its new A-class compact vehicle.
People throughout the day swarmed over a half-dozen models of the car inside the avant-garde open-air cube located on the city's Opernplatz, which is near the main shopping district.

The event, which even includes a play area for children and high-tech computers that highlight the car's safety features, was a far cry from past car introductions at which champagne and appetisers were in good supply at Mercedes showrooms.

The Frankfurt show will end on Saturday when the Catalan theatre company La Fura dels Baus, best known for "terrorising" audiences at a 1989 Sydney performance with chainsaws, shopping trolleys and offal, will be on hand for a show that encompasses the entire cube.

Mercedes, which spent $1.65 billion to design the A-class, needs the attention-grabbing controversial introduction to lure younger customers to the Mercedes brand in a bid to help expand its annual sales to one million vehicles by 2000.
But how many of the curious who visited the cube will buy the car remains to be seen as the models were sat in, poked and pressed, their doors being constantly opened and banged shut.
The A-class has been acclaimed in the automotive trade press for its technological and safety breakthroughs.
But some industry observers wonder whether the A-class may be too much of a departure from the existing Mercedes line and annoy loyal customers by clouding up the luxury brand image.

"The resonance so far has been very good," said Randi Maria Klages, who is managing the "A-Motion" introduction tour that will visit about 20 German cities and European capitals before the A-class is made available in dealer showrooms in October.

"There are certainly people around here who are interested in the A-class but there are also others who just want to take a look," she said amid the chaos as hundreds of people milled around the open-air stand made of wood and canvas.

An quick survey of the views of some visitors to the unorthodox stand, however, unveiled little interest among the throngs in buying the car but rather a desire to see how the venerable Mercedes can produce a car with a base price of about 30,000 marks ($17,400) -- more than half as cheap as many other Mercedes.

"It's a funny-looking car but I'm still curious and wanted to take a look at it," said Cifci Reza, a 24-year-old who could fit into Mercedes target market for the A-class -- namely singles, small families and young urban professionals.
"The image at first does not strike me as Mercedes but as Fiat or Renault," he said. "It's not the quality I would expect from Mercedes. And the price, well, it's awfully high."

Adolf Kalbfleisch, a 59-year-old resident of Frankfurt, said he would rather have the Polo made by Volkswagen AG than the A-class. VW's Polo is one-third the price and a few centimetres longer than the 3.60-metre-long A-class.
"If I had that much money to spend on a car, I would want more value and definitely more leg room," Kalbfleisch said. "Mercedes is a symbol for luxury, not for an economy vehicle."
But Martin Berghofer, who drives a Mercedes taxi around Frankfurt, disagreed, saying he was interested in the A-class after he retires in two years.
"I like the looks but I'll still wait some time for the problems to be worked out," Berghofer said.

Klages played down the critical comments, saying Mercedes had already taken firm customer orders since putting the car on sale last week. She also said hundreds, if not thousands, of people on Monday filled out cards seeking more information.
"This is a car that grows on you," she said. "A lot of people look at a car and quickly like it but the thrill then wears off. The A-class is one that really takes a hold of you."
